founded.what: The year an Épernay wine merchant of the Moët family founded the house, which took the name Moët & Chandon in 1833.

place: Épernay, Vallée de la Marne, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it owns vineyards, buys fruit from growers and makes the wine itself, and its labels carry the letters NM.

story: An Épernay wine merchant of the Moët family founded the house in 1743, and his grandson Jean-Rémy Moët (1758 to 1841) carried its wines across Europe; the Emperor Napoleon (1769 to 1821) visited him at Épernay and awarded him the Légion d'honneur. In 1833 the house passed to Jean-Rémy's son and his son-in-law, a Chandon, and took the name Moët & Chandon. In 1869 it created a non vintage Brut named Brut Impérial, by its own account a tribute to its ties with Napoleon. Its prestige cuvée honours Dom Pierre Pérignon, cellarer of the Benedictine abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until his death in 1715. The name had belonged to the house of Mercier, which passed it to Moët after a marriage between the two families in 1927. The first Dom Pérignon, from the 1921 vintage, was released in 1936, and the first Dom Pérignon Rosé came from the 1959 vintage. In 1971 Moët & Chandon joined the cognac house Hennessy as Moët Hennessy, and in 1987 Moët Hennessy merged with Louis Vuitton to form LVMH, by the group's own history. From the 1998 vintage the late releases of Dom Pérignon took the name P2, the second Plénitude.

style.line: Bright, fruity and consistent: the house speaks of bright fruitiness, a seductive palate and an elegant maturity, built by blending more than a hundred wines with a share of reserve wines, for ripe apple and pastry.
style.grapes: All three grapes in Moët Impérial, by the house: Pinot Noir 30 to 40 per cent, Meunier 30 to 40 and Chardonnay 20 to 30. Dom Pérignon is Chardonnay and Pinot Noir alone, chiefly from Grand Cru villages.
style.reserve: Moët Impérial is blended from more than 100 different wines, of which 20 to 30 per cent are reserve wines, by the house.
style.vessels: Dom Pérignon's base wines have fermented in stainless steel with no oak since the vintages after 1964, as the flagships record has it.
style.lees: Dom Pérignon rests on its lees for the better part of a decade before its first release, twelve to fifteen years and more before P2.
style.dosage: 7 grams a litre for Moët Impérial, by the house; low for Dom Pérignon, about 4.5 to 5 grams a litre for the 2015.

nv.name: Moët Impérial
nv.note: The non vintage Brut, created in 1869 as Brut Impérial, of Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay: the bottle most guests already know.

cuvee.name: Dom Pérignon

first.what: The first vintage, released in 1936, fifteen years after its harvest.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in the years the house declares, from the 1921 vintage on, so some years are skipped; the 2015 was released in 2024, with the 2006 as P2 beside it.
cuvee.blend: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir alone, in close to equal parts that shift with the year; no Meunier.
cuvee.sites: Chiefly Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, the Montagne de Reims and Aÿ, with fruit from the abbey's own Premier Cru vineyard at Hautvillers.
cuvee.making: Made only in declared vintages, from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir alone. Since the vintages after 1964 the base wines have fermented in stainless steel with no oak. The blend then ages on its lees for the better part of a decade before the first release: the 2015 was disgorged early in 2023 and released in 2024. The dosage is low, about 4.5 to 5 grams a litre for the 2015.
cuvee.lees: The better part of a decade before the first release; twelve to fifteen years and more before P2, and two decades and more before P3, as critics report the house.
cuvee.young: Toasted almond, white peach and fresh brioche, with a smoky note of struck flint and a fine, creamy mousse.
cuvee.aged: It moves towards roasted coffee, candied ginger and acacia honey, which is why the house releases the same vintage again as P2 and P3.

forms.name: Dom Pérignon Rosé
forms.note: The rosé of a declared year, made in far smaller quantity; its first vintage was 1959.

forms.name: Dom Pérignon P2
forms.note: The second Plénitude: the same vintage released again after twelve to fifteen years and more on its lees, first with the 1998, in place of the Œnothèque releases.

forms.name: Dom Pérignon P3
forms.note: The third Plénitude: the same vintage released after two decades and more on its lees.

cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

table.house45: Moët & Chandon is an Épernay house, founded in 1743 by a wine merchant of the Moët family. His grandson Jean-Rémy Moët welcomed Napoleon to Épernay, and the house took the name Moët & Chandon in 1833. In 1869 it created its non vintage Brut as Brut Impérial, a tribute to the Emperor. Guests know it as Moët Impérial, a blend of all three grapes from more than a hundred wines. The style is bright and fruity, with ripe apple and pastry. Dom Pérignon, named for the monk of Hautvillers and first released in 1936, is the house's prestige cuvée.
table.house10: Moët & Chandon is the Épernay house founded in 1743, the maker of Moët Impérial and of Dom Pérignon, first released in 1936.
table.cuvee45: Dom Pérignon, Moët & Chandon's prestige cuvée, carries the name of the Benedictine monk who kept the cellars of the abbey of Hautvillers. It is always a single vintage, made only in the years the house declares. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir go into it in close to equal parts, chiefly from Grand Cru villages. It rests in the cellar for the better part of a decade before release, and the same vintage comes back later as the second Plénitude. It shows toasted almond, white peach and fresh brioche, with a smoky note of struck flint. I pour it at 8 to 10 degrees, in a white wine glass.
table.sale: Named for the monk of Hautvillers, Dom Pérignon is one declared year of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, aged the better part of a decade. Would you like a bottle opened at the table?
table.cuvee10: Dom Pérignon is the prestige cuvée of Moët & Chandon: always one vintage, of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, first released in 1936.
table.cuvee20: Moët & Chandon makes Dom Pérignon only as a vintage and names it for the monk of Hautvillers. It is Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in close to equal parts, with toasted almond, white peach and a smoky note of struck flint.

guests.a: No. He was cellarer of the abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until 1715 and blended grapes from many vineyards; the tale that he invented the bubbles was first told in 1821, long after his death.

guests.q: Is Dom Pérignon made by Moët & Chandon?
guests.a: It has been Moët & Chandon's prestige cuvée since the first release in 1936. The name came to Moët from the house of Mercier after a marriage between the two families in 1927.

The second Plénitude: the same vintage of Dom Pérignon released again after twelve to fifteen years and more on its lees, deeper and more toasted. It took the place of the older Œnothèque releases, starting with the 1998.

guests.q: Is there a non vintage Dom Pérignon?
guests.a: No. Every Dom Pérignon is the wine of one year, and the label prints it. The house's non vintage wine is Moët Impérial.

traps: Dom Pérignon did not invent sparkling Champagne: he blended grapes from many vineyards, and the tale of his bubbles was first told in 1821.
Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon's prestige cuvée; Dom Ruinart is the prestige cuvée of Ruinart, of Reims. Both open on Dom, and they are different houses' wines.
P2 is not a different blend: it is the same vintage disgorged after a far longer stay on its lees.
Dom Pérignon is always vintage dated; Moët Impérial is the house's non vintage Brut, and Grand Vintage is the vintage wine under the Moët name.

sheet.label: Dom Pérignon
sheet.note: They agree. The label names the cuvée and its year; the house to pair it with in class is Moët & Chandon, whose prestige cuvée it has been since the first release in 1936.

questions.q: A guest asks for the prestige cuvée of Moët & Chandon on the class sheet. Which wine is it?
questions.exp: Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon's, first released in 1936. Dom Ruinart is Ruinart's prestige cuvée, La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's and Cristal is Louis Roederer's.

questions.q: In which year did the house take the name Moët & Chandon, passing to Jean-Rémy Moët's son and son-in-law?
questions.exp: The house took the name Moët & Chandon in 1833. It was founded in 1743, created Brut Impérial in 1869 and first released Dom Pérignon in 1936.

questions.q: On a Dom Pérignon label, what does P2 mean for the wine in the bottle?
opts: The same vintage released after far longer on its lees
A rosé blended with still red wine
A blend of several harvests with no vintage
A single vineyard wine of Hautvillers
questions.exp: P2, the second Plénitude, is the same vintage held twelve to fifteen years and more on its lees and released again. Dom Pérignon is never a blend of several harvests, and the rosé is a form of its own.

report: Built on the published flagships record (codex58, key moet-chandon, refuted 12 November 2026) and the library's p-moet-chandon and w-dom-perignon: no fact of them is contradicted, and the founder stays described, not named, as that refuter ruled.

Added from the house's own pages: Brut Impérial created in 1869 as a tribute to Napoleon, the Moët Impérial blend (Pinot Noir and Meunier 30 to 40 per cent each, Chardonnay 20 to 30), 20 to 30 per cent reserve wines among more than 100 wines, and 7 grams a litre.
The 1971 Moët Hennessy merger and the 1987 LVMH merger are dated by LVMH's own history page; the record says nothing of who holds the house today.

Lees: critics give eight to nine years from the harvest for the first Plénitude, twelve to fifteen and more for P2 and about twenty five for P3; the refuter set the record to the better part of a decade, twelve to fifteen and more, and two decades and more, as the published flagships record ruled.
Dom Pérignon 2015 dosage: 5 grams a litre by The World of Fine Wine and The Buyer, 4.5 by three merchants' sheets, so the record gives about 4.5 to 5; its disgorgement in 2023 is in several accounts.
Dom Pérignon Rosé: 1959 is its first vintage by Vinous, Wikipedia and Tastingbook; whether the 1959 was sold, and whether 1962 was the first sold, differ between accounts and are left out.

Left out for want of a source or because accounts differ: the hundred cases sent to New York in 1936 (one account says London in 1935), the story of the bottle and its shield shaped label (style.bottle is empty), and what MHCS on the back label stands for.
The plan asked how the label names its maker and how Dom Pérignon is presented beside Moët & Chandon: no page read states it, so the record tells it only as history, Moët's prestige cuvée since 1936.
style.malolactic is empty: no page read states it for Moët Impérial or Dom Pérignon.
kind.code: NM was read by the refuter from a Brut Impérial label's producer line, Épernay, France, NM 549 002, as Open Food Facts records it.

The library's p-moet-chandon calls the house the volume benchmark with the largest vineyard holdings, and the region record calls it the largest house: superlatives and present states this record does not repeat, listed for the owner.

changed: style.lees, cuvee.lees, making, table.cuvee45, table.sale: about seven to eight years before the first release became the better part of a decade, since critics give eight to nine from the harvest and the 2015 was disgorged early in 2023 (The Buyer, The World of Fine Wine), not after about eight years on its lees; the published flagships record words it the same way.

style.lees, cuvee.lees, forms[1], guests[2], questions[2].exp: about fifteen years before P2 became twelve to fifteen years and more, as two accounts give (Decanter, merchants), since the flagships refuter refused a single figure.
cuvee.rhythm: the 2013 and 2015 followed as first releases became the 2015 released in 2024 with the 2006 P2 beside it, a dated fact in place of a present list (The World of Fine Wine, The Buyer).
kind.means and report: NM read on a Brut Impérial label, NM 549 002 at Épernay, through Open Food Facts; the means now says the labels carry the letters.
table.house45: the house of Épernay became an Épernay house, so the line does not rank it.
sources: the house's own page on its history, whose facts the published flagships record already carries, gave way to the label record, to keep ten.
open: The Dom Pérignon Rosé's first vintage, 1959, stands; several accounts say the 1959 was never sold and the 1962 was the first sold, which the record does not tell.
The 2015's dosage stays about 4.5 to 5 grams a litre: most accounts give 5 and some merchants 4.5.
style.malolactic stays empty: no source read states it.
